title: Outcomes of Open Versus Endovascular Repair of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm Involving the Iliac Bifurcation.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Aneurysmal involvement of the iliac bifurcation increases the complexity of both open and endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), potentially raising the risk of postoperative complications. Randomized trials comparing endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) and open aortic repair (OAR) for AAA showed that EVAR is associated with a lower postoperative mortality rate. However, it remains unclear whether these results apply to AAA involving the iliac bifurcation (AAAIB). Several small single-institutional studies have shown conflicting results. This study aims to compare the outcomes of EVAR and OAR for AAAIB in a real-world, multi-institutional setting. METHODS: The Society for Vascular Surgery (SVS) Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI) database was queried for patients who underwent repair for AAAIB. The cohort was divided into 2 groups based on the intervention: EVAR versus OAR. Baseline demographic, clinical, and perioperative characteristics, as well as outcomes such as overall 30-day mortality, in-hospital mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: death, myocardial infarction, stroke), intestinal ischemia, overall reinterventions, and 1-year survival, were compared between the groups. Univariable analysis, multivariable inverse probability-weighted regression (IPWR), survival analysis with the Kaplan-Meier method, log-rank test, and Cox proportional hazards regression were performed. RESULTS: Of all reviewed patients, 7,535 were included in the final analysis, of whom 5,742 (76.2%) underwent EVAR, whereas 1,793 (23.8%) underwent OAR. In IPWR models, patients who underwent EVAR had significantly lower odds of overall in-hospital mortality (odds ratio [OR]: 0.25, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.18-0.34, P < 0.001), 30-day mortality (OR: 0.31, 95% CI: 0.23-0.42, P < 0.001), MACE (OR: 0.24, 95% CI: 0.19-0.31, P < 0.001), and other postoperative adverse events compared to OAR. The Cox proportional hazards model demonstrated a significantly higher 1-year survival rate for EVAR compared to OAR (hazard ratio [HR]: 0.61, 95% CI: 0.50-0.76, P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: In this real-world, multi-institutional study, EVAR for AAAIB was associated with lower odds of overall in-hospital mortality, 30-day mortality, MACE, as well as a higher 1-year survival rate, compared to the OAR. EVAR should be considered the primary method for repairing aortoiliac aneurysm involving the iliac bifurcation in anatomically suitable patients. Longer follow-up studies are needed to confirm these findings and compare the long-term reintervention and aorta-related mortality rates between the 2 treatment modalities.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Aneurysmal involvement of the iliac bifurcation increases the complexity of both open and endovascular repair of abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA), potentially raising the risk of postoperative complications. Randomized trials comparing endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) and open aortic repair (OAR) for AAA showed that EVAR is associated with a lower postoperative mortality rate. However, it remains unclear whether these results apply to AAA involving the iliac bifurcation (AAAIB).

title: Diagnostic Accuracy of the BlueDop Vascular Expert for Detecting Peripheral Arterial Disease in People with Suspected Intermittent Claudication Referred to Secondary Care: A Cross-Sectional Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Manual ankle-brachial pressure index (ABI) assessment reqiuires significant time and expertise, precluding its use in primary care. Automated vascular assessment tools may offer a simple and efficient alternative for detecting peripheral arterial disease (PAD). However, further evidence is needed before they can be recommended. This study considers the diagnostic accuracy of the BlueDop vascular expert (BVE) in people with suspected intermittent claudication. METHODS: We performed a cross-sectional cohort study including people referred to our nurse-led intermittent claudication clinic. BVE measurements were compared to the manual resting ABI/toe brachial index (TBI) method, using traditional cutoff values of <0.9 and < 0.7, respectively. RESULTS: 217 participants and 430 limbs were included, with an overall PAD prevalence of 46%. Sensitivity, specificity, positive predictor values (PPVs) and negative predictor values (NPVs) for the BVE were 88.5%, 80.7%, 81.3% and 88.1% respectively, when compared to the manual ABI. When compared to the manual TBI, the sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV for the BVE were 45.5%, 88%, 62.5%, and 78.6% respectively, though this analysis included only 38 limbs. No BVE diagnoses were based on ABI alone, 71% were based on waveform alone and 29% were based on a combination of ABI and waveform. The BVE assessment was significantly quicker to perform than the manual method (P < 0.01). CONCLUSION: The BVE demonstrated favorable sensitivity and specificity for detecting or excluding PAD compared to the manual ABI. Further work is needed comparing this device to others, across a range of clinical populations and settings before it can be considered in routine clinical practice.

Automated vascular assessment tools may offer a simple and efficient alternative for detecting peripheral arterial disease (PAD). However, further evidence is needed before they can be recommended.

title: Clinical outcomes of transperitoneal versus retroperitoneal approaches of open aortic repair for abdominal aortic aneurysm stratified by iliac bifurcation involvement.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Aortic aneurysm with iliac bifurcation involvement (AAAIB) is associated with higher rates of systemic comorbidities and increased complexity of open aortic repair (OAR), resulting in worse outcomes compared with OAR for isolated abdominal aortic aneurysm (IAAA). The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines recommend the retroperitoneal approach (RPA) for OAR in certain patients with abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA). However, there is limited evidence to determine whether the relative advantages and disadvantages of RPA and the transperitoneal approach (TPA) change depending on whether the aneurysm distally involves the iliac bifurcation. This study compared the outcomes of TPA and RPA for AAA, stratified by iliac bifurcation involvement, in a multi-institutional, real-world setting. METHODS: The Society for Vascular Surgery Vascular Quality Initiative database was queried for patients who underwent OAR for AAA from January 2003 to September 2024. Patients were stratified as having AAAIB or IAAA based on whether the aneurysm involved the iliac bifurcation and required a distal anastomosis beyond the common iliac artery bifurcation, or not. Baseline characteristics and clinical outcomes, such as overall 30-day mortality, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE: death, myocardial infarction, and stroke), and 1-year survival, were compared between the TPA and RPA groups in patients with IAAA and AAAIB. Univariable and multivariable analyses and a confirmatory analysis with inverse probability-weighted regression were performed. RESULTS: Of all the reviewed patients, 17,009 were included in the final analysis, of whom 15,218 (89.5%) had IAAA and 1791 (10.5%) had AAAIB. Among patients with IAAA, compared with RPA, TPA was associated with a higher odds of overall 30-day mortality (odds ratios [OR], 1.26; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.05-1.49; P = .011) and of MACE (OR, 1.26; 95% CI, 1.11-1.44; P = .001) and a lower 1-year survival rate (hazard ratio, 1.23; 95% CI, 1.09-1.39; P = .001). Among patients with AAAIB, TPA was associated with a lower odds of lower extremity ischemia (OR, 0.47; 95% CI, 0.25-0.91; P = .024), without significant differences in 30-day mortality (OR, 0.80; 95% CI, 0.42-1.51; P = .485), MACE (OR, 0.86; 95% CI, 0.52-1.42; P = .563), and 1-year survival (hazard ratio, 0.93; 95% CI, 0.59-1.47; P = .768). CONCLUSIONS: In this real-world study, iliac bifurcation involvement in AAA was an effect modifier for the outcomes of different OAR approaches. For patients with IAAA, compared with RPA, TPA was associated with worse 30-day mortality, MACE, and 1-year survival. In contrast, for patients with AAAIB, TPA was associated with a lower odds of lower extremity ischemia, without significant differences in 30-day mortality, MACE, or 1-year survival. This study suggests that RPA may be the procedure of choice for IAAA if it is otherwise feasible. However, TPA may be the procedure of choice for patients with AAAIB who are otherwise anatomically suitable. Larger prospective studies are warranted to validate these findings.

However, there is limited evidence to determine whether the relative advantages and disadvantages of RPA and the transperitoneal approach (TPA) change depending on whether the aneurysm distally involves the iliac bifurcation.

title: Imaging and Outcomes in the Treatment of Sacral Dural Arteriovenous Fistulas.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Spinal dural arteriovenous fistulas (DAVFs) in the sacral region are extremely rare, and their intradural retrograde draining system has not been investigated in detail. The aim of this study was to characterize the venous drainage patterns of sacral DAVFs based on our clinical experience in treating patients with this condition. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed the clinical data of patients with sacral DAVFs treated at our institution from January 2016 to January 2024. Preoperative spinal angiography was used to evaluate the positional relationship between the shunt point of sacral DAVF and the vertebral midline. We proposed that if the location of the shunt point was located on the midline, the draining vein would be the filum terminale vein (FTV); if the shunt point was located off the midline, the draining vein would be the radiculomedullary vein (RMV). RESULTS: A total of 17 patients with sacral DAVFs treated with direct surgery were included in this study. All patients presented with lower extremity weakness and numbness. Sphincter dysfunction was present in 15 patients (88.2%). The mean interval from the symptom onset to diagnosis was 14.1 months (range, 1-96 months). Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging detected T2 hyperintensity at the level of the conus medullaris and intradural flow voids in all patients. Spinal angiography confirmed the diagnosis of sacral DAVFs in all cases, and complete fistula occlusion was achieved with surgical ligation in all patients. Intraoperatively, 4 patients with the midline location of the shunt point were confirmed to have the FTV as the draining vein, whereas the other 13 patients with off-midline shunt point were confirmed to have the RMV as the draining vein. The intraoperative findings were completely consistent with the preoperative assessment of the draining veins based on the location of the shunt point. CONCLUSIONS: The draining veins of sacral DAVFs are not always the FTVs; in fact, most sacral DAVFs drain via the RMV. With our simple imaging-based method, the 2 different types of draining veins in sacral DAVFs can be preliminarily identified before surgery.

The aim of this study was to characterize the venous drainage patterns of sacral DAVFs based on our clinical experience in treating patients with this condition. METHODS: We retrospectively reviewed the clinical data of patients with sacral DAVFs treated at our institution from January 2016 to January 2024.

title: Anatomic Level as a Modifier of Racial/Ethnic Disparities in Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia: Outcomes after First-Time Endovascular Revascularization.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Racial and ethnic disparities in chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) outcomes are well documented, but whether these disparities vary by anatomic level of endovascular intervention remains unclear. We evaluated racial and ethnic differences in limb outcomes following endovascular revascularization for CLTI stratified by intervention level. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, including adults undergoing first-time lower extremity endovascular revascularization for CLTI between 2015 and 2024. Patients were stratified by intervention level: iliac, femoropopliteal, tibioperoneal, or combined femoropopliteal and tibioperoneal (multilevel). Propensity score matching balanced demographics and comorbidities across racial/ethnic cohorts. The primary outcomes were rates of 1-year major amputation and amputation-free survival. Outcome comparisons were reported as risk ratios (RRs). RESULTS: Among 14,786 patients, there were 3,071 iliac, 5,178 femoropopliteal, 2,363 tibioperoneal, and 3,718 multilevel interventions. After matching, Black patients demonstrated increased major amputation risk following iliac intervention (RR: 1.80, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.13-2.88, P = 0.012) and femoropopliteal intervention (RR: 1.83, 95% CI 1.39-2.41, P < 0.001) compared with White patients. No significant differences in amputation were observed following tibioperoneal or multilevel interventions. Hispanic patients exhibited increased amputation risk only in the multilevel cohort (RR: 1.57, 95% CI: 1.02-2.40, P = 0.037). Despite differences in amputation, amputation-free survival remained similar across racial and ethnic groups. CONCLUSION: Racial and ethnic disparities in CLTI outcomes following endovascular revascularization varied by anatomic intervention level. Disparities were most pronounced after proximal interventions and attenuated in distal disease, suggesting anatomic disease pattern may modify inequities in limb outcomes after revascularization.

We evaluated racial and ethnic differences in limb outcomes following endovascular revascularization for CLTI stratified by intervention level. METHODS: We performed a retrospective cohort study using the TriNetX US Collaborative Network, including adults undergoing first-time lower extremity endovascular revascularization for CLTI between 2015 and 2024.

title: Canadian Cardiovascular Society/Canadian Society of Cardiovascular Surgery/Canadian Association of Interventional Cardiology Clinical Practice Update on Transcatheter Mitral and Tricuspid Valve Intervention: Patient Evaluation and Management.
abstract: The management of mitral valve (MV) and tricuspid valve (TV) regurgitation has undergone significant transformation during the past decade. This change has been driven by a growing understanding of the adverse clinical consequences of these conditions, particularly their strong association with heart failure progression, reduced quality of life, and increased mortality-and by the emergence of effective transcatheter options for valve intervention. Among these, transcatheter MV edge-to-edge repair and replacement and transcatheter tricuspid edge-to-edge repair and replacement have become important therapeutic tools that provide a less invasive alternative to surgery in appropriately selected patients. In this clinical practice update we aim to provide contemporary, evidence-based guidance for clinicians in the evaluation and management of patients with severe, symptomatic MV or TV regurgitation who might benefit from transcatheter intervention. Key topics include the clinical presentation of these valve lesions, the diagnostic evaluation with emphasis on multimodality imaging and hemodynamics, criteria for patient selection, and current data on procedural and long-term clinical outcomes. A central theme is the role of timely referral and structured assessment to avoid missed opportunities for intervention. Optimal outcomes require active engagement from referring physicians and close collaboration within a multidisciplinary heart team, including cardiologists, cardiac surgeons, imaging specialists, heart failure specialists, and nursing partners-to ensure careful patient selection, procedural planning, and comprehensive post-intervention follow-up. By integrating clinical judgement with guideline-based recommendations and procedural expertise, transcatheter edge-to-edge repair or transcatheter valve replacement can offer substantial symptomatic relief and improved quality of life for selected patients, while minimizing procedural risk and enhancing overall cardiovascular outcomes.

title: One-Year Outcomes of Endovascular Repair of Zone 0/1 Aortic Arch Lesions With a Thoracic Branched Endoprosthesis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The GORE TAG thoracic branch endoprosthesis pivotal nonrandomized, multicenter, prospective trial evaluated 1-year outcomes in patients at high risk for open-surgical repair undergoing aortic arch and descending thoracic aorta endovascular repair (zone 0/1). METHODS: End points evaluated from endovascular procedure through 12 months included aortic-related death, disabling stroke, permanent paraplegia or paraparesis, new onset renal failure, and unanticipated reintervention. Core lab identified end points included aortic rupture or enlargement (≥5 mm), type I/III endoleak, device integrity, device migration, fistula, patency, and new dissection. RESULTS: The 77 patients enrolled had aneurysm (n = 50), dissection (n = 24), or other isolated lesion types (n = 3); 90.9% had a zone 0 proximal stent landing zone. Patients had a mean age of 70.8±10.8 years, 66.2% were men, and 57.1% were White. All had the aortic and side branch component implanted. Technical success was 94.8%. Early outcomes to 12 months included 8 aortic-related deaths (10.4%), 6 disabling strokes (7.8%, all in the aneurysm cohort), 4 unanticipated reintervention (5.2%), 2 aortic ruptures (2.6%), and 1 renal failure (1.3%). Type IA/IB or type III endoleaks occurred in 6 patients (7.8%). Loss of side branch patency occurred in 1 patient (1.3%). There was no permanent paraplegia or paraparesis or loss of device integrity or migration. A total of 5 patients had aortic enlargement; none required reintervention. CONCLUSIONS: Early data from this prospective investigation of the thoracic branch endoprosthesis device in zone 0/1 applications signal that the device is a reasonable therapeutic alternative in patients with appropriate anatomy deemed high risk for open arch surgery.

title: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair in hyperacute type B aortic dissection: a mini review.
abstract: Thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) is established as the preferred treatment for many patients with complicated acute type B aortic dissection (TBAD). However, its role during the hyperacute phase (within 24 hours of symptom onset) remains controversial, as the acutely dissected aortic wall may be vulnerable to device-related injury. Nevertheless, hyperacute timing should not be regarded as an absolute contraindication to TEVAR. In patients with rupture, malperfusion, impending aortic rupture, persistent pain, refractory hypertension, or progressive true-lumen collapse, prompt entry-tear coverage can restore perfusion and prevent irreversible organ injury. Similarly, in patients without initial complications, high-risk anatomical features may help identify those who could benefit from early intervention. However, evidence supporting routine TEVAR within the first 24 hours remains limited and is predominantly observational. To ensure safe hyperacute TEVAR, careful assessment of the landing zones, conservative device sizing, avoidance of aggressive balloon molding, preservation of branch-vessel and spinal cord perfusion, and prompt recognition of retrograde type A dissection, stroke, spinal cord ischemia, and stent-graft-induced new entry are required. Ultimately, hyperacute TEVAR may be a reasonable option for selected patients with complicated TBAD, with a potential role in high-risk uncomplicated TBAD. Future prospective randomized trials integrating multimodal imaging and dynamic biomarkers are warranted to establish definitive criteria for timing and candidate selection.

title: Venous Thromboembolism after Laparotomic and Laparoscopic Myomectomy with Large Myoma Burden.
abstract: STUDY OBJECTIVE: To investigate the incidence of venous thromboembolism (VTE) in patients undergoing myomectomy. To evaluate the impact of route of surgery, myoma burden, and operative time in the development of VTE in this population. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study (Canadian Task Force Classification II2) of targeted myomectomy data from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program. SETTING: National Surgical Quality Improvement Program Database. PATIENTS OR PARTICIPANTS: Women aged ≥18 years undergoing laparotomic and laparoscopic myomectomy between 2011 and 2022. Patients were classified by current procedural terminology codes as having low or high myoma burden (>250 g or >4 fibroids). Patients undergoing hysterectomy, vaginal or hysteroscopic myomectomy, with malignant pathology, or missing operative time were excluded. INTERVENTIONS: Cases were identified by current procedural terminology codes. Variables including age, ethnicity, body mass index, smoking status, diabetes, hypertension, blood transfusion, inpatient status, and American Society of Anesthesiologists classification system scores were collected. Clinical predictors of VTE were evaluated by stratifying cases according to surgical route, operative time, year of procedure, and myoma burden. MEASUREMENTS AND MAIN RESULTS: A total of 38 167 myomectomies occurring between 2011 and 2022 were included. Of these, 20 943 (54.9%) patients underwent laparotomy, and 17 224 (45.1%) patients underwent laparoscopy. The incidence of VTE after myomectomy was 0.28%. Patients undergoing laparotomy had twice the VTE rate (0.36%) compared with those undergoing laparoscopy (0.18%). Patients undergoing laparotomy were more likely to be younger, of non-Hispanic African American ethnicity, inpatient, with higher body mass index, require blood transfusion, have higher myoma burden, and have shorter operative times. After multivariable adjustment, neither myoma burden nor surgical route was independently associated with VTE. However, longer operative time (>186 minutes, 75 percentile) was independently associated with increased odds of VTE (adjusted odds ratio 2.73; confidence interval: 1.52-4.90). CONCLUSION: The occurrence of VTE after laparoscopic and laparotomic myomectomy is uncommon. The rate of VTE is higher with longer operative times, but this outcome is not significantly associated with surgical route or myoma burden.

To evaluate the impact of route of surgery, myoma burden, and operative time in the development of VTE in this population. DESIGN: Retrospective cohort study (Canadian Task Force Classification II2) of targeted myomectomy data from the American College of Surgeons National Surgical Quality Improvement Program.

title: Limb Salvage Outcomes Following Endovascular Revascularization for Peripheral Artery Disease in a Southern Indian Population: A Single-Center Retrospective Study.
abstract: Background Peripheral artery disease (PAD), particularly chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), is associated with a high risk of limb loss and significant morbidity. Endovascular therapy (ET) has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative to surgical revascularization, especially in high-risk patients and those with comorbidities. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of ET in achieving limb salvage in a Southern Indian population. Materials and methods This retrospective observational study was conducted at a tertiary vascular care center and included 142 patients with symptomatic PAD who underwent endovascular intervention between July 2023 and June 2025. Clinical severity and lesion complexity were assessed using the Rutherford classification and the TransAtlantic Inter-Society Consensus II (TASC II) classification, respectively. The primary endpoint was limb salvage at one year, defined as freedom from major amputation. Secondary endpoints included technical success, restenosis, and procedure-related complications. Results The study population was predominantly male (87.3%) with a mean age of 61.11 ± 12.90 years. Most patients (78.1%) presented with CLTI. Technical success was achieved in 87.3% of procedures. At one-year follow-up, limb salvage was achieved in 95.8% of patients, with major amputation occurring in 4.2% and minor amputation in 9.1%. Restenosis was observed in 14.7% of cases. Procedure-related complications were infrequent and mostly minor, with one all-cause death during follow-up. Conclusions ET is a safe and effective modality for limb salvage in PAD patients, particularly in populations with a high prevalence of diabetes and advanced disease at presentation. High limb salvage rates can be achieved even in cohorts predominantly comprising patients with CLTI, supporting an endovascular-first approach in appropriately selected patients.

Endovascular therapy (ET) has emerged as a minimally invasive alternative to surgical revascularization, especially in high-risk patients and those with comorbidities. This study aims to evaluate the effectiveness of ET in achieving limb salvage in a Southern Indian population.

title: Multicenter outcomes of peripheral vascular interventions in patients with active cancer.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Cancer is typically associated with venous thrombosis, but its impact on patients undergoing peripheral vascular interventions (PVIs) for concomitant peripheral arterial disease remains unclear. This multicenter study examines the characteristics of patients with active cancer and their outcomes after PVI. METHODS: Institutional Vascular Quality Initiative PVI data from three tertiary care centers (2019-2023) were combined and expanded through a retrospective chart review to include the presence and types of cancer. All adult patients undergoing endovascular intervention for peripheral arterial disease, including those with claudication, chronic limb-threatening ischemia, and acute limb ischemia, were included. The primary outcome was the composite of major amputation or mortality at 4 years in patients with cancer compared to those without. Additional long-term outcomes included reintervention, mortality, and major amputation at both 1 and 4 years. Secondary outcomes included perioperative outcomes. RESULTS: A total of 3072 patients were included. The incidence of active cancer was 2.2% (N = 68). Lung cancer was the most common, affecting 30.9% (N = 21) of patients. 53% (N = 36) presented with advanced stages (3/4) irrespective of cancer type. Patients with cancer were less likely to have diabetes. There was no significant difference in indication, but patients with cancer were more likely to get treated for aortoiliac disease and undergo stenting. Patients with cancer had a higher incidence of distal embolization (4.4% vs 0.6%; P = .012) and perioperative major amputation (4.4% vs 1.3%; P = .046). Kaplan-Meier analysis showed significantly higher mortality or amputation in patients with cancer up to 4 years (63% vs 35.1%; P < .001). Late outcomes in patients with cancer were driven by significantly higher mortality (52.2% vs 28.3%; P < .001) rather than adverse limb events (amputation: 14.7% vs 11.4%, P = .50; reintervention: 47.8% vs 48.3%, P = .80). Regression analysis demonstrated independent association of cancer with the composite outcome of mortality or major amputation (adjusted hazard ratio, 2.24; 95% confidence interval, 1.61-3.10). CONCLUSIONS: Active cancer affects a small proportion of patients undergoing PVI but has a significant impact on perioperative limb outcomes and long-term survival. This multicenter collaboration, combining registry data and electronic medical record review, can shed light on less common risk factors affecting lower-extremity revascularization.

title: Outcomes among patients with single-vessel tibial runoff undergoing revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia, and the role of peroneal communicating branch quality.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Data evaluating outcomes among patients with single-vessel tibial runoff are limited. Our aim was to compare outcomes across patients with sole anterior tibial (AT), peroneal, or posterior tibial (PT) runoff following revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), and to evaluate whether the quality of peroneal communicating branches (PCBs) affects outcome risk within the peroneal runoff population. METHODS: All patients undergoing first-time revascularization for CLTI were retrospectively reviewed (2005-2022) and stratified by sole runoff vessel (AT, peroneal, and PT). Primary outcomes were wound healing, major amputation, major adverse limb events (MALE), and amputation/death, assessed by Kaplan-Meier analysis and multivariable Cox regression. A subset analysis stratified single-vessel peroneal runoff patients into a three-tiered, PCB grade: Both branches present with at least one robust (PCB grade 1), a single robust branch (PCB grade 2), or no robust branch (PCB grade 3), and compared each with the single-vessel AT/PT reference group. RESULTS: Overall, 732 patients had single-vessel below-knee runoff: 225 AT, 315 peroneal, and 192 PT. Groups differed significantly in age, sex, and diabetes prevalence. Unadjusted 2-year major amputation rates were significantly higher in the peroneal group [19% vs 9.4% (AT) vs 8.7% (PT); P < .001], as were MALE rates (30% vs 14% vs 26%; P = .01). After adjustment, peroneal runoff was independently associated with higher risk of major amputation [hazard ratio (HR), 1.81; 95% confidence interval (CI), 1.04-3.13] and MALE (HR, 1.52; 95% CI, 1.03-2.25) compared with AT/PT runoff. These associations persisted in the endovascular cohort (major amputation: HR, 2.09; 95% CI, 1.06-4.13; MALE: HR, 1.59; 95% CI, 1.08-2.35) but did not reach significance in the bypass cohort, which was limited by low-event rates. When patients with single-vessel peroneal runoff were stratified by PCB grades, unadjusted 1-year major amputation rates followed a clear anatomically-driven pattern [6.9% (AT/PT) vs 5.4% (PCB grade 1) vs 15% (PCB grade 2) vs 32% (PCB grade 3); P < .001]. After adjustment, when compared with AT/PT runoff, patients without any robust branch (PCB grade 3) had significantly higher risk of major amputation (HR, 3.21; 95% CI, 1.76-4.84) and MALE (HR, 2.41; 95% CI, 1.53-3.79), whereas those with two communicating branches with at least one being robust (PCB grade 1) demonstrated higher rates of complete wound healing (HR, 1.69; 95% CI, 1.09-2.62) and no difference in major amputation or MALE. CONCLUSIONS: Peroneal runoff is independently associated with worse limb outcomes following revascularization for CLTI, but this risk may be primarily driven by patients with absent or diminutive communicating branches. Patients with robust branching demonstrate outcomes comparable with AT/PT runoff, underscoring the importance of further evaluation and preoperative assessment of PCB quality - using the proposed PCB grading system - in revascularization planning.
englishSummary: OBJECTIVES: Data evaluating outcomes among patients with single-vessel tibial runoff are limited. Our aim was to compare outcomes across patients with sole anterior tibial (AT), peroneal, or posterior tibial (PT) runoff following revascularization for chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI), and to evaluate whether the quality of peroneal communicating branches (PCBs) affects outcome risk within the peroneal runoff population. METHODS: All patients undergoing first-time revascularization for CLTI were retrospectively reviewed (2005-2022) and stratified by sole runoff vessel (AT, peroneal, and PT).

title: Hypoxia and right ventricular dysfunction in patients with acute pulmonary embolism.
abstract: BACKGROUND: In patients with acute pulmonary embolism (PE), hypoxia may increase pulmonary vascular resistance and worsen right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), which is a key prognostic factor. However, associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes have not been well described. AIM: To describe associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes in patients with PE. METHODS: We performed a retrospective, single-center cohort study of patients treated by the Massachusetts General Hospital Pulmonary Embolism Response Team (PERT) from 10/2012 to 08/2021. Inclusion criteria included confirmed PE, recorded oxygen saturation prior to PERT activation, and echocardiogram within three days of PERT activation. Patients were categorized into four subgroups based on (1) hypoxia status (SaO₂ below vs. above 95%) and, (2) oxygen support (below vs. above 3 L/min). Our primary outcome was the presence of RVD on echocardiogram. Our secondary outcome was clinical deterioration within 7 days. RESULTS: We included 894 PE patients. The mean age was 61 (± 16 SD), 614/894 (69%) were hypoxic, and 624/894 (70%) had RVD on echocardiogram. Overall, hypoxic patients were more likely to have RVD than non-hypoxic patients (467/614 [76%] vs. 157/280 [56%], p < 0.0001). On subgroup analysis, RVD prevalence was highest in the "hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L" group (n = 216/266, 81%) followed by the "not hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L" group 53/70 (76%); 198/278 (71%) in the "hypoxic with oxygen support <3L" and 157/280 (56%) in the "not hypoxic with oxygen support <3L" groups. Clinical deterioration occurred in 199/894 (22%) patients and was more common in hypoxic patients than non-hypoxic patients (157/614 [26%] vs. 42/280 [15%], p < 0.0001), and most common in the "hypoxic with oxygen support ≥3L" subgroup 88/266 (33%). CONCLUSIONS: Hypoxia is associated with RVD and clinical deterioration in patients with PE. More research is needed to understand the risk associated with hypoxia and the physiology of supplemental oxygen support in PE. CLINICAL TRIAL NUMBER: Not applicable.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: In patients with acute pulmonary embolism (PE), hypoxia may increase pulmonary vascular resistance and worsen right ventricular dysfunction (RVD), which is a key prognostic factor. However, associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes have not been well described. AIM: To describe associations between hypoxia, RVD and clinical outcomes in patients with PE.

title: A comparison of aspiration thrombectomy with catheter-directed thrombolysis in the management of Paget-Schroetter syndrome.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Acute subclavian vein thrombosis secondary to thoracic outlet syndrome (Paget-Schroetter syndrome [PSS]) requires the prompt clearing of thrombus from the subclavian vein through catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) or aspiration thrombectomy (ASP). Our goal is to systematically compare the outcomes of CDT and ASP in the management of PSS. METHODS: Consecutive patients with PSS at a single institution from 2020 through 2025 were reviewed for management with CDT or ASP. Venograms were assessed for patency, stenosis, and subclavian post-thrombotic changes (PTC). PTC were graded based on the degree of luminal encroachment and vessel irregularity: mild (<10%), moderate (10%-50%), and severe (50%-99%). Interventions were assessed: (1) within 1 week of the procedure, (2) before subclavian vein decompression, (3) 2 weeks after subclavian vein decompression, and (4) patency on the last venogram. Standardized outcomes were assessed. RESULTS: A total of 110 patients with PSS were treated over 5 years. Of these patients, 54 met the inclusion criteria: 28 underwent CDT and 26 underwent ASP. At 1 week following the procedure, rethrombosis occurred in 1 (3.6%) patient who underwent CDT and 6 (23.1%) patients who underwent ASP (P < .5). Failure to clear thrombosis occurred in 13.8% of patients who underwent ASP. The composite rate of early thrombosis and procedural failure was higher in the ASP cohort. Before PSS surgery, occlusion was noted in 1 (3.6%) patient who underwent CDT and 8 (30.8%) patients who underwent ASP (P < .05). PTC was mild in 13 (46.4%) patients receiving CDT and 5 (19.2%) receiving ASP (P < .05); moderate in 5 (17.9%) receiving CDT and 5 (19.2%) receiving ASP; and severe in 9 (32.1%) receiving CDT and 8 (30.8) receiving ASP. At early follow-up after PSS surgery, PTC was mild in 10 (43.5%) patients receiving CDT and 4 (23.5) receiving ASP; moderate in 2 (8.7%) receiving CDT and 1 (5.9%) receiving ASP; and severe in 9 (39.1%) receiving CDT and 6 (35.3%) receiving ASP. Occlusion was noted in 2 (8.7%) patients receiving CDT and 6 (35%) receiving ASP. Recanalization resulted in final patency in 22 (95%) patients receiving CDT and 15 (88%) receiving ASP. CONCLUSIONS: Both ASP and CDT may be employed for clearing thrombus in PSS; however, they differ in early efficacy, PTC, and patency. Our results suggest that while often more rapid and convenient, ASP may be inferior to CAT in the management of PSS.

Our goal is to systematically compare the outcomes of CDT and ASP in the management of PSS. METHODS: Consecutive patients with PSS at a single institution from 2020 through 2025 were reviewed for management with CDT or ASP.

title: Faculty narrative feedback in the vascular surgery entrustable professional activity pilot is disproportionately focused on patient care and medical knowledge competencies.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: Performance feedback is critical to guide vascular surgery trainees' skill development across competency domains. Workplace-based assessment of entrustable professional activity (EPA) allows faculty frequent opportunities to provide and document clinical performance feedback. Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) Milestones were previously mapped to each EPA and accompanying behavioral anchors reflect the range of competencies required to execute each clinical activity. It is unclear how faculty use this information to guide and focus the content of their feedback. We sought to identify the core competencies reflected in narrative feedback in a multi-institutional study of EPA assessments. METHODS: EPA assessments were collected during a 3-month national Vascular Surgery EPA Pilot in 2024. Trainees were rated on their performance of EPAs on a 4-point Likert scale and faculty had the opportunity to provide feedback. Narrative feedback was qualitatively analyzed using focused coding guided by the Vascular Surgery Milestones 2.0 framework. Feedback was coded using the six ACGME core competencies-patient care (PC), medical knowledge (MK), professionalism, interpersonal and communication skills, practice-based learning and improvement, and systems-based practice (SBP)-to characterize the domains emphasized in feedback. Quality assessment scores were assigned to all narrative feedback using the Quality of Assessment of Learning framework. Descriptive analysis was completed using R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing). RESULTS: Faculty completed 983 EPA assessments of 78 trainees across 17 institutions (n = 16 integrated residencies, n = 12 fellowships). Narrative feedback was included in 760 (77%) assessments. Feedback most frequently addressed PC (n = 662, 82%), followed by MK (n = 418, 55%), whereas feedback about practice-based learning and improvement (n = 42, 6%), interpersonal and communication skills (n = 42,6%), professionalism (n = 20, 3%), and SBP (n = 26, 3%) were less common. Most assessments were completed for postgraduate year-3 (29%) and postgraduate year-4 trainees (22%). Most assessments occurred during the intraoperative phase of care (88%), with relatively few occurring in preoperative (7%) or postoperative (5%) phases. In addition, feedback-referencing PC was associated with higher odds of high-quality feedback in comparison with feedback about the other competencies (odds ratio, 25.56; 95% confidence interval, 6.13-106.55). CONCLUSIONS: In this multi-institutional study of vascular surgery EPA assessments, faculty most frequently provided trainees with feedback on their performance of PC and MK competencies. Feedback on performance related to SBP was infrequently provided and, when provided, was of generally low quality. This has important implications for the use of EPAs to inform ACGME Milestones ratings and suggests alternative assessment tools will continue to be needed to capture performance across all competency domains required of a physician.
englishSummary: OBJECTIVES: Performance feedback is critical to guide vascular surgery trainees' skill development across competency domains. Workplace-based assessment of entrustable professional activity (EPA) allows faculty frequent opportunities to provide and document clinical performance feedback. Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education (ACGME) Milestones were previously mapped to each EPA and accompanying behavioral anchors reflect the range of competencies required to execute each clinical activity.

title: Association of Estimated Arterial Stiffness with Collateral Status and Functional Outcome after Endovascular Thrombectomy: A Secondary Analysis of the OPTIMAL-BP Trial.
abstract: PURPOSE: Estimated pulse wave velocity (ePWV) is a surrogate of arterial stiffness that may influence stroke outcomes and potentially affect collateral circulation. We examined the association of ePWV with collateral status and 3-month functional outcome after successful endovascular thrombectomy and explored the contribution of collateral status to this relationship across blood pressure (BP) management strategies. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this secondary analysis of the Outcome in Patients Treated With Intra-Arterial Thrombectomy-Optimal Blood Pressure Control trial, 285 patients were analyzed. Collateral status was assessed using the Tan scale (poor, 0-1; good, 2-3). Poor functional outcome was defined as 3-month modified Rankin Scale score of 3-6. Multivariable logistic and mediation analyses were performed to evaluate the association between ePWV and functional outcomes and to explore direct and indirect pathways. RESULTS: A total of 285 patients were included (mean age, 73.3±11.3 years; 40.4% women). Each 1 m/s increase in ePWV was associated with poor collaterals (adjusted odds ratio [OR] 1.276, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.083-1.503) and poor functional outcome (adjusted OR 1.338, 95% CI 1.121-1.597). In mediation analyses, collateral status accounted for only a small proportion of the association between ePWV and poor functional outcome (indirect effect: adjusted β 0.022, 95% CI 0.001-0.053), whereas the direct effect remained significant (adjusted β 0.237, 95% CI 0.115-0.359). Neither the direct effect of ePWV on functional outcome nor the indirect effect through collateral status differed according to BP management strategy. CONCLUSION: Higher ePWV was associated with poor collateral status and unfavorable functional outcome after successful reperfusion. Collateral status accounted for only a small proportion of the observed association between ePWV and functional outcome.

We examined the association of ePWV with collateral status and 3-month functional outcome after successful endovascular thrombectomy and explored the contribution of collateral status to this relationship across blood pressure (BP) management strategies. MATERIALS AND METHODS: In this secondary analysis of the Outcome in Patients Treated With Intra-Arterial Thrombectomy-Optimal Blood Pressure Control trial, 285 patients were analyzed.

title: Beyond Absolute Blood Pressure Targets During Endovascular Thrombectomy: A Narrative Review of Intraprocedural Hemodynamics.
abstract: Hemodynamic management is a central component of procedural care for acute ischemic stroke (AIS) during endovascular thrombectomy (EVT). Current guideline recommendations predominantly provide absolute blood pressure (BP) targets for intraprocedural management. Studies have also examined relative BP reduction, the magnitude and duration of hypotensive exposure, and blood pressure variability (BPV), providing additional measures of systemic hemodynamic exposure during EVT. However, definitions, baseline reference pressures, measurement intervals, and BPV metrics vary widely across studies, and associations with neurological outcomes are inconsistent. Importantly, these systemic BP parameters do not directly establish cerebral perfusion. This limitation supports investigating cerebral autoregulation as a complementary, patient-specific assessment. Evidence linking individualized autoregulatory limits to outcomes remains predominantly post-EVT, with very limited evidence during the pre-recanalization phase under anesthesia. This review examines intraprocedural BP during EVT under anesthesia beyond absolute pressure targets. It considers relative BP reduction, the magnitude and duration of hypotensive exposure, pressure-time burden, BPV, and individualized autoregulatory limits in relation to cerebral perfusion. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed for studies evaluating hemodynamics during EVT under anesthesia, supplemented by screening of selected reference lists. Studies examining intraprocedural BP targets, relative changes, hypotension duration, pressure-time burden, and BPV in relation to neurological or imaging outcomes under anesthesia were prioritized, with emphasis on the pre-recanalization period. Post-EVT hemodynamic studies were not included in the primary synthesis, except where they informed the discussion of cerebral autoregulation and future research. Intraprocedural hemodynamic variables during EVT characterize different aspects of systemic arterial-pressure exposure that may be relevant to cerebral perfusion in the ischemic penumbra. Absolute pressure, relative change, magnitude and duration of hypotension, pressure-time burden, and BPV should be regarded as complementary rather than interchangeable measures. Differences in reference pressures, definitions, measurement intervals, exposure periods relative to recanalization, and anesthesia techniques limit comparisons and standardization across studies. Future prospective studies, particularly during general anesthesia (GA), should integrate clearly defined systemic BP metrics with dynamic cerebral autoregulation. This may help determine which parameters or combinations best reflect cerebral physiological vulnerability. Individualized autoregulation-guided BP targets remain investigational and require prospective validation before they can inform routine clinical hemodynamic management.

Current guideline recommendations predominantly provide absolute blood pressure (BP) targets for intraprocedural management. Studies have also examined relative BP reduction, the magnitude and duration of hypotensive exposure, and blood pressure variability (BPV), providing additional measures of systemic hemodynamic exposure during EVT.

title: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement in bicuspid versus tricuspid aortic valves among patients with mixed aortic valve disease.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Mixed aortic valve disease (MAVD), defined as the coexistence of significant aortic stenosis (AS) and aortic regurgitation (AR), presents unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Prior studies rarely distinguished bicuspid valve morphology in MAVD populations, and no study has evaluated long-term transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR) outcomes between bicuspid aortic valve (BAV) and tricuspid aortic valve (TAV) patients in this setting. The aim is to investigate the clinical outcomes of BAV versus TAV morphology in patients with MAVD undergoing TAVR. METHODS: Between March 2013 and December 2024, 610 MAVD patients undergoing TAVR were included. Patients with severe AS and concomitant presence of moderate or more severe aortic regurgitation were defined as the MAVD. Clinical outcomes, functional status and echocardiography were followed and compared. RESULTS: A total of 610 patients were included in this study, 220 (36.1%) of whom were BAV morphology. BAV patients were younger (73 vs. 75 years, p < 0.001) and had a lower Society of Thoracic Surgeons (STS) score (3.47% vs. 4.15%, p < 0.001) compared to TAV patients. The five-year mortality rate was lower in bicuspid than tricuspid patients (10.5% vs. 18.7%, log-rank p = 0.014), while Cox regression analysis did not indicate BAV as an independent predictor of five-year all-cause mortality after multivariable adjustment (hazard ratio [HR] 0.75, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.47-1.22, p = 0.253). During the one-year follow-up after procedure, BAV patients exhibited a greater increase in AVA and LVEF (p for interaction = 0.012 and 0.011, respectively), and a greater reduction in mean gradient and peak velocity (both p for interaction < 0.001). Meanwhile, similar left ventricular reverse remodelling was found during follow-up (both p for trend < 0.001). CONCLUSIONS: In MAVD patients undergoing TAVR, bicuspid and tricuspid valve morphologies demonstrated comparable long-term clinical outcomes. BAV patients demonstrated greater improvements in left ventricular function and transvalvular hemodynamics, suggesting that bicuspid morphology itself does not confer an adverse long-term prognostic effect in appropriately selected patients with MAVD undergoing TAVR. title: Endovascular repair of iatrogenic popliteal artery injury with acute limb ischemia during unicompartmental knee arthroplasty.
abstract: Iatrogenic popliteal artery injury is a rare but severe complication of knee arthroplasty. A 75-year-old woman developed massive bleeding and acute limb ischemia during unicompartmental knee arthroplasty. Angiography showed severe popliteal flow impairment with thrombus and absent distal runoff. Because bleeding was controlled and guidewire crossing appeared feasible, an endovascular-first strategy was chosen. After successful crossing, an intravascular ultrasound scan confirmed severe arterial wall disruption and an adequate distal landing zone. VIABAHN stent grafts excluded the injured segment, and tibial thrombus aspiration restored distal perfusion. The patient was discharged without gait impairment. Endovascular-first treatment may be effective in selected patients.

A 75-year-old woman developed massive bleeding and acute limb ischemia during unicompartmental knee arthroplasty. title: One-year outcomes of mechanical thrombectomy and catheter-directed thrombolysis in acute pulmonary embolism.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Although anticoagulation remains the standard of care for acute pulmonary embolism (PE), mechanical thrombectomy (MT) and catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) have emerged as effective interventional options for rapid clot removal. However, their comparative outcomes remain incompletely defined. Hence, this study compared the outcomes of MT and CDT for acute PE at a tertiary referral center in the United States. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of all patients who underwent MT or CDT for acute PE across a single hospital system between January 2021 and April 2025. Patients were stratified into MT and CDT groups based on the treatment received. Baseline characteristics, procedural data, and clinical outcomes were analyzed. The primary outcome was 30-day mortality. The secondary outcomes included length of hospital stay, major adverse events, reintervention, and PE recurrence. Patients were followed up for up to 1 year or until death. RESULTS: A total of 724 patients were included in this study: 569 (79%) underwent MT and 155 (21%) received CDT. The mean age was 63 ± 16 years, and 49% were female. Most patients (76%) were classified as intermediate-high risk, with a mean right ventricle to left ventricle ratio of 1.5 ± 0.5. Bilateral or saddle embolism was present in 93% of patients. Patients in the MT group were more likely to have a simplified PE severity index of >0 (73% vs 60%; P < .001). Age and the rates of cancer, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, and concurrent deep vein thrombosis were similar between the groups. The median procedure duration was longer for MT (66 minutes, interquartile range, 46-89) than for CDT (58 minutes, interquartile range, 40-77; P = .003). The median postoperative length of stay was 3 days in both groups. MT was associated with a higher incidence of intraoperative adverse cardiac events (2.5% vs 0%; P = .048), and CDT was associated with higher intensive care unit admission rates (83% vs 36%; P < .001). However, the 30-day mortality rate was similar between the groups (CDT: 2.6% vs MT: 4.6%; P = .27). Additionally, the 1-year incidence rates of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (MT: 4.5% vs CDT: 3.4%; P = .69), PE recurrence (MT: 4.4% vs CDT: 2.5%; P = .31), and all-cause mortality (MT: 7.8% vs CDT: 5.8%; P = .41) were not statistically significantly different between the MT and CDT groups. CONCLUSIONS: In this retrospective cohort, MT and CDT for acute PE showed statistically comparable 30-day mortality rates and 1-year recurrence rates of chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension and PE. MT was associated with a higher incidence of intraoperative cardiac complications, and CDT was associated with more frequent intensive care unit admission.
englishSummary: BACKGROUND: Although anticoagulation remains the standard of care for acute pulmonary embolism (PE), mechanical thrombectomy (MT) and catheter-directed thrombolysis (CDT) have emerged as effective interventional options for rapid clot removal. However, their comparative outcomes remain incompletely defined. Hence, this study compared the outcomes of MT and CDT for acute PE at a tertiary referral center in the United States.

title: Antiphospholipid syndrome: epidemiology and outcomes in the evolving criteria era.
abstract: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a heterogeneous autoimmune thrombo-inflammatory disorder characterized by thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity and an expanding spectrum of microvascular, cardiac, haematological and other systemic manifestations. Although research has provided considerable insights into the pathogenesis and clinical phenotypes of APS, its epidemiology remains difficult to define because estimates depend on case definitions, antibody testing, repeat-testing requirements, testing practices and data sources. Population-based studies suggest that APS is rare, and catastrophic APS is rarer and best understood through registry data. Antiphospholipid antibody positivity alone does not establish APS; transient or low-level positivity can occur without disease, whereas persistent antibodies must be interpreted alongside compatible clinical manifestations. Despite its rarity, APS causes substantial morbidity through recurrent thrombosis, organ damage and adverse pregnancy outcomes, supporting targeted evaluation in unprovoked or recurrent venous thromboembolism, stroke in younger adults and selected pregnancy complications. Apparent differences among populations can reflect ascertainment, access to testing, study design and biological variation. Standardized case definitions, antibody testing and laboratory reporting, together with longitudinal population-based research in ancestry-diverse, paediatric and low-income and middle-income populations, are needed to refine estimates of APS burden and define its clinical spectrum.

title: A Compact Unified Model for Moderate-to-Severe Carotid Artery Stenosis Using Image Segmentation: A Multicenter Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: This study aimed to evaluate the diagnostic performance of a new artificial intelligence model, the compact unified model (CU-Model), for moderate-to-severe carotid artery stenosis using digital subtraction angiography (DSA) images compared to clinical reference standards. METHODS: In this retrospective multicenter study, 156 patients with confirmed moderate-to-severe carotid artery stenosis were included. A pretrained CU-Model (trained on public non-clinical datasets for optical flow and stereo matching) was applied to raw DSA images without any fine-tuning on clinical data to avoid data leakage. The model served exclusively as a post-acquisition support tool: cardiologists applied it immediately after procedures for automated vessel segmentation and highlighting. Final North American Symptomatic Carotid Endarterectomy Trial (NASCET) measurements and interpreta-tions were performed manually under expert supervision by 2 blinded researchers. RESULTS: The CU-Model identified left internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis in 84 patients and right ICA stenosis in 72. It misclassified only 1 moderate left ICA stenosis case as normal, achieving 99.4% sensitivity (155/156) for any stenosis detection. For stenosis severity grading, strong agreement with DSA was observed (moderate: 57.68 ± 5.94 vs. 57.71 ± 6.19, r = 0.83, P < .001, 95% CI: 0.76-0.88; severe: 86.96 ± 5.97 vs. 87.02 ± 6.18, r = 0.91, P < .001, 95% CI: 0.85-0.95). Of 156 cases, 106 were moderate (50%-69%) and 50 severe (≥70%), using NASCET-adapted thresholds accounting for measurement variability. Hypertension (77%), smoking, and syncope were common, with significant association in symptomatic patients (P < .05). CONCLUSION: The CU-Model demonstrates strong concordance with DSA as a practical, post-procedure support tool for vessel segmentation. Pending larger validation studies, it shows promise for enhancing clinical workflow efficiency.

title: Use of smart glasses for ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization in adults: a randomized clinical trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Head-mounted displays can be integrated with ultrasonography to overlay the image in the operator's field of view, improving hand-eye coordination during invasive procedures. The clinical efficacy of smart glasses for central venous catheterization (CVC) remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether using smart glasses can improve efficiency compared to conventional ultrasound-guided CVC. METHODS: This prospective, single-blinded, controlled study enrolled adult patients who underwent elective surgery requiring CVC. Patients were assigned to either the ultrasound screen (control) or smart glasses group using stratified randomization according to operator qualification. The primary outcome was the overall CVC procedural time. Secondary outcomes included ultrasound scanning and venous access time, number of needle redirections and probe repositionings, procedural success and complication rates. RESULTS: In total, 124 patients were analyzed. The overall procedural time was significantly reduced in the smart glasses group compared to that in the control group (158 [140, 189] s vs. 134 [117,150] s; median difference, 26.0 s; 95% CI, [16.0-37.0] s, P < 0.001). Specifically, the ultrasound scanning time (median difference, 3.0 s, P = 0.004), venous access time (median difference, 2.0 s, P = 0.013), number of needle redirections (median difference, 1.0, P = 0.003) and probe repositionings (median difference, 0.0, P = 0.005) were significantly reduced in the smart glasses group compared to those in the control group. However, the success and complication rates were comparable between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Smart glasses modestly improved procedural efficiency in ultrasound-guided CVC, potientially for novices, without improving success or complication rates. Larger-sample studies with more diverse operators and patients are warranted. title: Endovascular Management With a Fenestration Technique of an Iatrogenic Thoracic Chronic Type B Aortic Dissection.
abstract: We report the case of an 86-year-old woman who developed an intraoperative type B aortic dissection during ascending aortic replacement for an ascending aortic aneurysm. Postoperative imaging demonstrated an uncomplicated dissection extending to the infrarenal aorta. At 10 weeks, follow-up imaging revealed rapid aneurysmal expansion of the false lumen. Thoracic endovascular aortic repair was performed with adjunctive cerebrospinal fluid drainage, rapid pacing, and image fusion guidance. An intimal fenestration technique was used to optimize the distal sealing zone, extending the disruption from a pre-existing re-entry tear. A type Ib endoleak necessitated additional stent-graft deployment, which in turn caused occlusion of the left renal and superior mesenteric arteries. The STABILISE technique (stent-assisted balloon-induced intimal disruption and relamination in aortic dissection repair) with a PETTICOAT (Provisional Extension To Induce Complete Attachment) bare stent restored renal perfusion, and targeted stenting re-established mesenteric flow. A postprocedural pseudoaneurysm was managed conservatively and resolved with spontaneous thrombosis within 48 hours. The patient was discharged on postoperative day seven, asymptomatic, with complete exclusion of the dissection, patent visceral vessels, and no endoleak confirmed at six-week follow-up. This case illustrates that combining distal flap fenestration with STABILISE relamination and a comprehensive endovascular toolkit can successfully manage complex chronic type B aortic dissections, even in elderly, high-risk patients-provided that adequate perioperative safety measures and a broad endovascular armamentarium are available to address unanticipated complications.

Postoperative imaging demonstrated an uncomplicated dissection extending to the infrarenal aorta. At 10 weeks, follow-up imaging revealed rapid aneurysmal expansion of the false lumen.

title: Detection of serum amyloid A in Saliva of patients with internal carotid artery stenosis: a pilot study.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine whether serum amyloid A (SAA) is detectable in saliva of patients with internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis and to investigate the relationship between salivary and serum SAA levels across the perioperative period of carotid endarterectomy (CEA). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Six patients with asymptomatic ICA stenosis (60-99%) undergoing CEA were enrolled. Periodontal status was assessed at enrolment and used to characterise the cohort and document potential oral inflammatory confounding of salivary SAA. Salivary and serum SAA, C-reactive protein (CRP), and lipid parameters were measured before CEA, on postoperative day 2, and 30-45 days postoperatively using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and standard laboratory methods. RESULTS: SAA was detectable in all saliva samples. Serum SAA increased after surgery and did not decline at follow-up, whereas salivary SAA showed a progressive decline (repeated measures ANOVA: F(2,4) = 25.01, p = 0.005). A strong negative correlation was observed between changes in serum and salivary SAA (Pearson's r = - 0.976, p = 0.004). CONCLUSIONS: In this small pilot cohort, SAA was detectable in all saliva samples, and salivary concentrations decreased across the perioperative time points while serum SAA did not show a parallel decline. The observed inverse serum-saliva association should be interpreted cautiously given the very small sample size, absence of a control group, and potential oral and sampling confounders. These findings support the feasibility of measuring salivary SAA in this clinical setting and warrant confirmation in larger controlled studies.

title: Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Hospitalized Medical Patients: A Narrative Review of Risk Stratification, Treatment Duration, and Bleeding Trade-Offs.
abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains a leading preventable cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized medical patients, yet decisions about who should receive prophylaxis - and for how long - remain far from settled. This review synthesizes evidence from 22 sources, including randomized trials, prospective and retrospective cohorts, systematic reviews, and major society guidelines, addressing risk stratification, in-hospital anticoagulant prophylaxis, extended-duration direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), the associated bleeding trade-offs, and real-world implementation. The evidence broadly supports pharmacologic prophylaxis during hospitalization for appropriately selected, acutely ill medical patients with acceptable bleeding risk, with the strongest randomized evidence favoring low-molecular-weight heparin during the inpatient period. That benefit comes with trade-offs worth weighing carefully, since even well-supported regimens carry a measurable increase in bleeding risk alongside their protective effect. Commonly used risk-assessment tools have real limitations as well: the Padua and IMPROVE scores offer a useful clinical framework, but head-to-head comparison shows both discriminate poorly between patients who will and won't develop VTE, and real-world implementation data reveal frequent misclassification and inconsistent dose administration. Extended-duration anticoagulation after discharge follows a similar pattern across the major DOAC trials in this space - fewer thrombotic events, but more bleeding, without a clear survival benefit. Taken together, this evidence points toward a risk-adapted rather than protocol-driven approach: assess VTE and bleeding risk at admission, initiate appropriate inpatient prophylaxis, reassess as the clinical picture changes, confirm that prescribed doses are actually being given, and reserve extended anticoagulation after discharge for carefully selected patients rather than applying it as a default. Meaningful progress in this area will likely come less from another static risk score and more from models that can track mobility, bleeding risk, and treatment response dynamically over the course of a hospital stay.

title: Interventional Management of Patients with Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Portal Vein Tumor Thrombosis: Are There Differences Between East and West?
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review summarizes current evidence on interventional therapies for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT), compares the treatment strategies between East and West, and proposes a practical framework for patient selection in the immunotherapy era of HCC. RECENT FINDINGS: Although systemic therapy remains the primary treatment for advanced HCC with PVTT, selected interventional therapies may provide additional value in carefully chosen patients with preserved liver function, liver-dominant disease, anatomically targetable PVTT, and adequate or reconstructable portal venous flow. Interventional options include transarterial chemoembolization, hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy, transarterial radioembolization/selective internal radiation therapy, radiotherapy, portal vein stenting, and iodine-125 seed-based endovascular brachytherapy. Eastern and Western practice patterns differ mainly in the threshold for locoregional intensification, technical platform availability, and interpretation of the available evidence. Eastern and Western approaches increasingly share the principle that systemic therapy is the treatment backbone for advanced HCC with PVTT. The key clinical question is how interventional therapy should be integrated for selected patients rather than whether it should replace systemic therapy. Optimal management should be individualized through multidisciplinary decision-making based on PVTT extent, portal venous flow, liver function, intrahepatic and extrahepatic tumor burden, treatment goals, and institutional expertise. Future studies should standardize reporting of PVTT classification, portal vein patency, collateral circulation, liver reserve, tumor distribution, systemic therapy context, and treatment sequencing.

title: Selective endovascular aortic repair in connective tissue disease patients within a multidisciplinary program achieves comparable outcomes in high-risk patients.
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVE: Endovascular aortic repair (ENDO) in patients with connective tissue disease (CTD) has historically been discouraged in society guidelines because of durability concerns. However, high-volume aortic centers increasingly employ ENDO strategies in carefully selected high-risk patients across scenarios such as rupture, dissection-related pathology, or hostile anatomy. Herein, we describe temporal ENDO adoption at our multidisciplinary CTD aortic program. METHODS: In this study, 92 patients with CTD undergoing aortic intervention at a single high-volume aortic center between 2005 and 2023 were analyzed. Patients were stratified by ENDO (n = 50) vs open repair (OPEN; n = 42). The primary outcome was freedom from aortic-related mortality (ARM). The secondary outcomes included technical success, complications, secondary aortic intervention (SAI), and overall survival. A prespecified contemporary analysis (2018-2023) was conducted to evaluate the outcomes following the establishment of a multidisciplinary CTD aortic program. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate survival and freedom from SAI. RESULTS: The mean age was 48 ± 16 years, and 34% (n = 31) were female. Diagnoses included Marfan syndrome (69%), Loeys-Dietz syndrome (15%), familial aortopathy (11%), and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (5%). Patients who underwent ENDO more frequently had prior sternotomy/open cardiac surgery (68% vs 19%; P < .0001), prior aortic surgery (70% vs 33%; P = .0007), and urgent presentation (50% vs 14%; P = .0004). Overall, 60% of these patients were deemed unfit for open repair by the multidisciplinary aortic team because of physiologic risk, anatomic complexity, or urgent presentation. The technical success rate was lower after ENDO (82% vs 98%; P = .02), and the 30-day reintervention rate was higher (16% vs 0%; P = .01). The median follow-up period was 2.3 years [interquartile range, 1.1-4.7]. SAIs occurred more frequently following ENDO (56% vs 12%; P = .0001), including planned staged procedures (ENDO: 28.6% vs OPEN: 20%; P = 1) and unplanned reinterventions (ENDO: 71.4% vs OPEN: 80%; P = 1). In the full cohort, patients undergoing ENDO had lower 3-year survival rates (71% ± 7% vs 92% ± 4%; log-rank P = .03). In the contemporary cohort, survival at 2 years following ENDO (n = 17) was poorer than that after OPEN (n = 42), although the difference did not reach significance (71% ± 14% vs 92% ± 4%; log-rank P = .1). Similarly, the rate of freedom from ARM was lower, but not significantly different (88% ± 12% vs 98% ± 2%; log-rank P = .4). CONCLUSIONS: Open repair remains the gold standard for connective tissue disease-associated aortic disease. In carefully selected high-risk patients, ENDO serves as a complementary strategy with acceptable contemporary survival and comparable freedom from ARM. Higher secondary intervention rates reflect both planned staged repair and unplanned surveillance-detected failure modes, underscoring the need for lifelong follow-up within multidisciplinary programs.

However, high-volume aortic centers increasingly employ ENDO strategies in carefully selected high-risk patients across scenarios such as rupture, dissection-related pathology, or hostile anatomy. Herein, we describe temporal ENDO adoption at our multidisciplinary CTD aortic program.

title: Closing the Gap in Thromboprophylaxis: A Multidisciplinary Quality Improvement Approach Among Medical Inpatients.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the impact of a multidisciplinary quality improvement (QI) framework on guideline-directed venous thromboembolism (VTE) prophylaxis adherence among hospitalized patients. STUDY DESIGN: A prospective, pre-post interventional study conducted in internal medicine wards with historically low baseline prophylaxis rates. METHODS: Following a retrospective baseline assessment, a multicomponent QI initiative was executed across 2 Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles in adult internal medicine wards at a university hospital between September and November 2022. Interventions included the following: (1) physician education on the Padua Prediction Score and International Medical Prevention Registry on Venous Thromboembolism Bleeding Risk Score; (2) implementation of an electronic health record clinical decision-support tool prompting VTE risk assessments; and (3) integration of clinical pharmacists into daily multidisciplinary rounds to provide active audit and feedback. RESULTS: At baseline, 62.1% of high-risk patients received guideline-recommended VTE prophylaxis. Post intervention, this rate increased to 79.1% in the first cycle and 82.1% in the second cycle ( P  = .006). Among clinical pharmacists' 27 recommendations, 70.4% were accepted and implemented. The multidimensional strategy demonstrated sustained improvements in guideline adherence with minimal adverse events. CONCLUSIONS: Implementing a multidisciplinary QI framework significantly enhanced guideline-directed VTE prophylaxis use among hospitalized patients. This collaborative approach underscores the value of electronic decision support, clinical audit-feedback loops, and pharmacist-physician integration in driving patient safety. Ultimately, this system-level strategy provides a scalable model for improving preventive care protocols across diverse hospital settings.

METHODS: Following a retrospective baseline assessment, a multicomponent QI initiative was executed across 2 Plan-Do-Study-Act cycles in adult internal medicine wards at a university hospital between September and November 2022.

title: Artificial intelligence for the detection of large vessel occlusion stroke and workflow optimization: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: To evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) tools on workflow efficiency, treatment times, and clinical outcomes in patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke. METHODS: We included observational studies that assessed the implementation of AI-based tools in the management of patients with suspected or confirmed LVO stroke. Eligible studies reported workflow, treatment, safety, or functional outcomes. Data were extracted on thrombolysis rates, CTA-to-arterial puncture time, door-to-puncture time, endovascular treatment (EVT) access, reperfusion success, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH), mortality, and functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days. Random-effects models were applied to calculate pooled mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Thirteen studies were included. AI implementation significantly reduced workflow delays: CTA-to-puncture time decreased by -40.20 minutes (95% CI -66.41 to -13.99; P<0.01) and door-to-puncture time by -23.17 minutes (95% CI -38.71 to -7.63; P<0.01). Thrombolysis administration showed no difference (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.57-1.09; P=0.15). Similarly, no significant effects were observed for EVT access (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.66-1.44; P=0.89), reperfusion success (RR 1.06; 95% CI 1.00-1.12; P=0.06), sICH (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.30-1.35; P=0.23), or mortality (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.38-1.37; P=0.32). However, AI-based workflows significantly improved functional independence at 90 days (RR 1.55; 95% CI 1.12-2.15; P=0.008). CONCLUSIONS: AI tools significantly improve treatment times and functional independence in acute LVO stroke without increasing adverse events.

METHODS: We included observational studies that assessed the implementation of AI-based tools in the management of patients with suspected or confirmed LVO stroke. Eligible studies reported workflow, treatment, safety, or functional outcomes.

title: Incremental prognostic and risk-stratification value of ultrasound-based Carotid Plaque Reporting and Data System (Plaque-RADS) classification for recurrent ischemic stroke in patients with low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Carotid Plaque Reporting and Data System (Plaque-RADS) is a system for stroke risk assessment. However, the clinical utility of ultrasound (US)-based Plaque-RADS remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the incremental prognostic value and risk stratification utility of US-based Plaque-RADS in patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis. METHODS: Between January 2020 and December 2022, 231 patients with carotid plaque ipsilateral to the prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis were retrospectively screened, of whom 158 were included in the final analysis. US-based Plaque-RADS classification was assigned based on duplex US assessment of plaque features. Cox regression and subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the association between high-risk US-based Plaque-RADS categories and recurrent ischemic stroke. Model discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curves and area under the curve (AUC), and clinical utility was evaluated using decision curve analysis. The association between increasing US-based Plaque-RADS categories and the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke was assessed by trend analysis. The incremental risk-stratification value of refined high-risk Plaque-RADS thresholds was quantified with net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling. RESULTS: vs. During the 3-year follow-up period, recurrent ischemic stroke occurred in 33 patients. High-risk US-based Plaque-RADS categories were significantly associated with recurrent ischemic stroke in patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis, after adjusting for smoking, homocysteine, and intraplaque neovascularization [adjusted hazard ratio: 3.56; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.07-11.83, P=0.038]. No statistically significant interactions were observed across the subgroups (all P for interaction >0.05). The Plaque-RADS ≥3 model demonstrated a higher AUC than the conventional US model [0.816 (95% CI: 0.731-0.901)0.810 (95% CI: 0.720-0.899)] and provided a slight net benefit across selected threshold probabilities. Additionally, the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke increased with higher Plaque-RADS categories (P for trend <0.001). Among the models using different high-risk Plaque-RADS thresholds, the Plaque-RADS ≥3b model showed the best predictive performance (0.865, 95% CI: 0.799-0.930), compared with the Plaque-RADS ≥3 model and the Plaque-RADS ≥3c model [0.824 (95% CI: 0.740-0.906)]. The Plaque-RADS ≥3b model also showed moderate improvements in NRI [0.250; (95% CI: 0.088-0.557), P=0.017] and IDI [0.090; (95% CI: 0.000-0.185), P=0.049], compared with the Plaque-RADS ≥3 model. Bootstrap internal validation indicated limited optimism across all models. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis, high-risk US-based Plaque-RADS categories were significantly associated with recurrent ischemic stroke. The US-based Plaque-RADS may help identify plaque phenotypes associated with an increased risk of recurrent ipsilateral ischemic stroke, while refined high-risk thresholds, particularly Plaque-RADS ≥3b, may provide additional value for risk stratification.

However, the clinical utility of ultrasound (US)-based Plaque-RADS remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the incremental prognostic value and risk stratification utility of US-based Plaque-RADS in patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis.
